1	---
2	name: prose-to-checks
3	description: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
4	---
5	
6	# Convert existing prose to checks
7	
8	A completeness-critic over a repo's own packs: prose that is always-testable but was never converted
9	becomes a check, so the packs keep shedding context over time instead of only at the moment a rule is
10	first learned.
11	
12	## Two callers, differing only in scope
13	
14	- **The upgrade pass**, as the last step of a
15	  [growth-extract](../../tasks/growth-extract/task.md) run: the scope is the prose **that run just
16	  wrote**. Extraction already descends the promotion ladder per lesson, but a lesson written as prose
17	  under time pressure is exactly where a convertible rule hides, so it gets asked once more before the
18	  PR opens. Never widen from here into the standing backlog.
19	- **The weekly [prose-to-checks-sweep](../../tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md)**: the scope is the
20	  **standing backlog** — everything under the pack paths configured for this repo, which the task
21	  passes in its Context. A consuming repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/`) by
22	  default — projects don't improve core canon packs — while **Claudinite itself** also sweeps its core
23	  `packs/`. Read the prose under those paths (each pack's `RULES.md`, and any `SKILL.md` beside them).
24	
25	Plus on demand, when someone asks. Either way: never edit a read-only mounted canon pack under
26	`.claudinite/shared/`. Everything below is identical for both callers.
27	
28	## First gate — a working rule, not a product statement
29	
30	Before asking whether a rule is *testable*, ask whether it belongs to a pack at all: **does it govern
31	how we work, or state what the product does?** A pack — canon or local — homes the conventions,
32	gotchas and review discipline that recur across tasks whatever the feature happens to be. A rule
33	asserting which entities exist, what a surface must render, or that a feature's parts are wired to
34	each other is a **requirement**; its home is the project's executable spec and the suite that proves
35	it (the full rule lives in
36	[generate-project-instructions](../generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md)).
37	
38	This gate comes **first** because product statements sail through the check-the-world test below —
39	"this module must export `X`" has an obvious static signature. Converting one splits a feature's
40	definition across two systems and lands half of it in the one no test of the product ever reads.
41	Load-bearingness is not the test: a real gap in product coverage is a *requirements* gap. Neither is build
42	quality — a product statement converts into a genuinely well-made check, clean parse and see-it-fail proof and
43	all, and is still the wrong kind. The discriminator, applied **before** you write anything: *if the product
44	changed its mind tomorrow, would this rule be wrong?* Wrong → it's a requirement, and a red check would report
45	a product decision as a process violation. Still true whatever the product decides → it's a working rule.
46	
47	A product statement already sitting in pack prose is mis-homed, and a sweep is not the place to
48	re-home it. **Leave the prose and log it** as a mis-homed rule, the same way an un-checkable
49	candidate is logged — never cement it as a check.
50	
51	## What to look for — the check-the-world test
52	
53	For each rule that cleared the gate, ask the one question from
54	[engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md): **does it constrain a *static
55	signature in the repo artifact* — something a post-hoc scan could observe?**
56	
57	- **Yes → a conversion candidate.** A dangling-reference rule, a filename convention, a workflow
58	  or manifest shape, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code.
59	- **No → leave it.** In-flight process (leaves no artifact — "see the test fail first"),
60	  judgment ("name by scope"), or knowledge whose failure is only visible at runtime (jsdom
61	  diverging from Chrome). These are why the rule is prose; don't force them.
62	
63	**"Already covered by another check" is a claim to test, not to reason out** — hand the sibling check a file
64	that violates the rule before dropping the candidate as a duplicate. A ban list only covers the routes whoever
65	wrote it thought of, so the routes it misses are invisible to exactly the reasoning that drew it: three sweeps
66	running dropped an "the app opens no socket" rule because a neighbouring check banned the obvious networking
67	import, while the base library re-exported a raw socket call that sailed straight through.
68	
69	**"Not statically checkable" is a verdict about the tree's shape when it was taken, not about the rule —
70	re-derive it against today's sources.** A removal, a migration or a consolidation can collapse the entry points
71	a rule had to cover, and the objection dies with them: a "one deletable storage directory" rule needed
72	data-flow tracing while many entry points wrote paths, and needed none once one root remained. So when a sweep
73	meets prose an earlier sweep left behind, re-ask the question rather than trusting the recorded answer. (This
74	covers the *technical* verdict only — an owner's rejection of a conversion is settled.)
75	
76	**Read the conversion tracker's prior comments before authoring, not after.** Independent re-derivation is
77	exactly how duplicate work happens: a fresh reading of the same prose will happily re-nominate a rule, build it
78	out in full, and only then discover it was built and rejected before. The tracker is a precondition of the
79	work, not a place to log it — and record each rejection with its reason so the next run can act on it.
80	
81	**A static signature is necessary, not sufficient.** Both shapes the working-discipline rules bar
82	— a rule that pins today's code in place, and one derivable from the product's requirements —
83	answer *yes* here, so screen every candidate against that bar before converting it. Leave either
84	where it is; routing a requirement to the spec and its suite is its own change, not this sweep's.
85	
86	The check-the-world rule from DESIGN holds: if a rule is always-testable, it was never really
87	part of the on-demand skill — it belongs in a pack as a check.
88	
89	## How to convert one
90	
91	Follow the extract stage's check-authoring discipline (the local promotion ladder in
92	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). For each candidate:
93	
94	> **The upgrade-pass caller lands inside growth-extract's own PR**, which auto-merges after CI — so the
95	> see-it-fail fixture is the only gate a converted check gets there. Convert only what you can prove;
96	> anything shakier stays prose and waits for the weekly sweep's reviewed PR.
97	
98	1. **Author the check** in the owning pack (`<pack>/<rule>.mjs`, listed in its `pack.mjs`) — the
99	   failure message *is* the rule (what / why / fix / `doc:` pointer back to the prose).
100	2. **Write the fixture first and see it fail** — a violating fixture must find, a clean one must
101	   not (the test lives beside the pack's other tests). A conversion with no proving fixture
102	   doesn't ship.
103	3. **Ship at real severity, fail-fast** — blocking for a defect, advisory when the rule is
104	   directional by kind, or when the condition is blocking-grade but **irreversible by the time it is
105	   observable** (an append-only transcript, a published artifact). A blocking finding no edit can
106	   retract never converges — it spends every remaining Stop cycle on something nothing can fix.
107	   Advisory there is *diagnostic*: it names the cause the moment it appears.
108	   - **Prefer a positive allowlist over an enumerated list of the bad cases.** Match the one allowed
109	     shape and flag everything else, rather than banning the violations you can name. An allowlist
110	     catches a variant that doesn't exist yet the day it lands, and turns an indirection (a value
111	     passed through a variable instead of written literally) into a finding too — refusing to reason
112	     about indirection is the feature. Invert only where the allowed set is genuinely open-ended.
113	4. **Delete the prose the check now covers** — whole, never trimmed. The deletion test below is
114	   how you decide which paragraphs those are.
115	
116	**Before writing a rule off as un-checkable, try parsing the file's structure instead of grepping
117	its text.** Grep finds the pattern anywhere; parsing finds it in the one spot the rule means —
118	which kills the false alarm. (Example: `Authorization` is only wrong inside a CloudFront policy's
119	*own* header list, not elsewhere in the template.) Parse only as much as you need, and hold the
120	check to the same fixture bar.
121	
122	**When a rule mandates a *form*, the check asserts that form — never the intent behind it.** Where
123	the prose says *write it exactly like this*, the check's whole job is deciding whether the artifact
124	is that form; inferring what the author meant is unbounded in the wrong direction and leaves the
125	likeliest reproduction uncaught, since a hand-picked marker list always misses the phrasing nobody
126	enumerated. Expect a form check to fire on something that breaks the form while causing no harm —
127	that's the rule as written doing its job, not a reason to re-add intent-guessing.
128	
129	When even a scoped parser can't make detection confident, **leave the prose and log the
130	candidate** to a tagged conversion-backlog issue rather than shipping a shaky check.
131	
132	## Coming out: the deletion test
133	
134	Coming out of a conversion, apply the **deletion test**: prose a mechanism fully covers is
135	deleted, never trimmed. Ask it of every paragraph standing beside a landed check — *with this
136	paragraph gone, would the check still catch every violation it describes **and** tell the agent
137	how to fix it?* If yes, it is redundant: delete it whole. The check's failure message is where
138	the rule lives now and its header comment is where the rationale lives, so a paragraph restating
139	either pays twice and is the drift trap waiting to spring.
140	
141	Before concluding prose is the only carrier, look at the pack's **skills** too — an
142	activity-scoped skill often already holds the map a rule is repeating. Keep only what no artifact
143	carries.
144	
145	The test **discriminates** rather than just deleting: a paragraph stays whole whenever it carries
146	something the check does not — a second rule in the same breath, an exemption the check can't
147	encode, a value the check can't judge, or a remedy the finding's own `fix` line never states
148	(a finding renders `what` / `why` / `fix` / `doc`, never the rule's `description`, so a remedy
149	that lives only in the description is not carried). Two worked calls: an `npm test` invariant
150	went entirely — the check caught it and the testing-guide skill already listed the suites —
151	while an `extension-test/` mirror bullet stayed, because the check beside it enforced only the
152	`package.json` list's sync with the tree and never the mirror convention itself.
153	
154	Whether a check covers a rule is a judgment about meaning, so this test is applied by a
155	**reader**, not mechanized.
156	
157	## Bounds
158	
159	- **One PR, bounded surface** — the new rule module, its `pack.mjs` line, its fixture, and the
160	  trimmed prose. Don't "improve" unrelated rules while you're in there.
161	- **Never delete a rule you didn't convert** — the deletion test is only ever asked of a rule a
162	  *landed* check now enforces.
163	- Run the suite and the sweep green before the PR goes up, and never push to `main` directly. The
164	  sweep opens its own PR for the owner's approval; the upgrade pass adds its conversion to the
165	  growth-extract PR already being opened, and opens none of its own.

input.new_string:
## A GitHub MCP list/search read blows the token cap — `fields` is the size knob, `per_page` is not

Any `mcp__github__*` read that returns a *list* of objects here returns the objects whole,
and the result is routinely 80KB–400KB — over the cap, so nothing reaches the session and
the body is spilled to a `tool-results/*.txt` file instead. Eight captured sessions between
2026-07-30 and 2026-08-12 hit it twelve times, across four different tools:
`search_repositories` (80KB, 86KB), `pull_request_read` `get` (158KB, 157KB, 168KB),
`search_issues` (112KB, 106KB) and `actions_list` `list_workflow_runs` (395KB, twice).

The trap is that the obvious knob is the wrong one. On 2026-08-12 a session called
`actions_list list_workflow_runs` with `per_page: 5`, got the overflow, and retried 23s
later with `per_page: 3` — **exactly 395,103 characters both times.** `per_page` does not
shrink these payloads; the per-object field set does. So:

- Pass a **`fields` subset** on every `search_issues` / `list_issues` / `search_repositories`
  call — `["number","title","state"]` is enough for almost everything Claudinite tasks do.
  Dropping `body` alone is usually the whole difference; the same session's third
  `search_issues` call, identical but for `fields`, came back fine.
- `actions_list` has **no `fields` and no `minimal_output`** — `per_page` is its only knob and
  it doesn't work. Don't retry it smaller. Either narrow with `workflow_runs_filter`, or take
  the overflow as the answer and query the spilled file directly
  (`python3 -c "import json; …"` or `jq` over the `tool-results/*.txt` path in the error).
  That fallback is what finally worked, ~35s after the first attempt.
- For a PR, prefer the narrow method (`get_files`, `get_commits`, `get_check_runs`) over
  `get`, whose body plus every field is what overflows.

## Never use WebFetch to obtain content you must have

1	# Delivering a scheduled task's pull request
2	
3	How an executor subagent delivers the PR its task produced — the AGENT lane of the one
4	delivery procedure. The CODE lane is `land-pr.mjs` beside this file (Action-side workers
5	run it); **the two must keep saying the same thing** — a nuance changed in one changes in
6	the other in the same commit. Your GitHub writes go through the session's MCP tools, and
7	your pushes ride a credential whose events start workflows normally, so — unlike the code
8	lane — your PR's checks need no help from you to run.
9	
10	## The task sets the ceiling; the repo decides the rest
11	
12	Your task's declared `expected_outcome` is a **ceiling, not a plan**:
13	
14	- **`open-pr`** — open the PR and stop. Never arm auto-merge, never merge. Nothing below
15	  applies to you.
16	- **`merged-pr`** — the task *may* land its PR. Whether it actually lands unreviewed is
17	  **this repo's** setting, read in step 1 — never the task's own knowledge. The same task
18	  lands itself on one repo and waits for an owner on another, and both are correct.
19	
20	## 1. Read the repo's delivery preference
21	
22	`.claudinite-checks.json` → `maintenance.delivery`:
23	
24	- **`auto-merge`** (legacy aliases `auto`, `push`) — go to step 2.
25	- **`review`** (legacy alias `pr`) — leave the PR open for the owner and stop. Never arm
26	  it, never merge it, and never read the standing PR as a failure: degrading `merged-pr`
27	  to open-pr is the repo's stated intent, and member config wins.
28	- **Missing or empty** — proceed as `auto-merge` (the default). Do **not** write the key:
29	  materializing it is baselining's converge job, not yours.
30	- **Anything else** — someone stated an intent you cannot honour, and guessing could
31	  deliver its opposite. Leave the PR open (the posture that merges nothing) and name the
32	  unrecognized value in your wrap-up comment on the dispatch issue.
33	
34	## 2. Arm auto-merge
35	
36	Arm GitHub's native auto-merge on the PR — **squash**, always. Armed → done: GitHub lands
37	it once this repo's required checks pass.
38	
39	## 3. When the arm is rejected
40	
41	- **"Pull request is in clean status"** — the base branch requires nothing, so auto-merge
42	  has no queue to wait behind and this arm will be rejected every time. That is a repo
43	  *shape*, not an error — nothing needs fixing, and the merge is yours to make: once any
44	  checks that did start on the PR's head have **concluded green**, merge it yourself
45	  (squash). A repo with no PR checks at all merges as soon as the PR is mergeable.
46	- **Any other rejection** ("auto-merge is not allowed", "unstable status", …) — judge on
47	  evidence, exactly as the code lane's landing pass does. Read the workflow runs on the
48	  PR's **head sha**:
49	  - A run parked at `action_required` **never ran** — it is neither a pass nor a failure;
50	    ignore it and judge by the runs that actually executed.
51	  - Wait (within your run's time budget) for the real runs to conclude. Everything
52	    concluded, nothing failed, at least one succeeded → merge (squash).
53	  - Anything genuinely failed (`failure`, `timed_out`, `cancelled`, `startup_failure`),
54	    or the runs won't conclude inside your budget, or GitHub refuses the merge itself
55	    (a required gate you could not see) → **leave the PR open** and say why in your
56	    wrap-up comment, naming the repo settings a human should check: Settings → General →
57	    "Allow auto-merge", and Settings → Actions → General workflow-approval requirements
58	    (the usual source of the parked `action_required` run). A PR left open with its
59	    reason stated is a *delivered* outcome within the `merged-pr` ceiling — the trail
60	    survives and the task's next cycle (or the owner) picks it up; a merge past a red or
61	    unseen check does not survive anything.
62

64	
65	Merge with anything but squash; merge while a real check is failing or still running;
66	arm or merge when the repo said `review`; write `maintenance.delivery` yourself; or
67	manufacture a merge to satisfy the ceiling — "no change" and "left open, reason stated"
